content.text:
Operator
Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Welcome to the Q1 2024 Matador Resources Company Earnings Conference Call. My name is Daniel, and I'll be serving as the operator for today. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. We will facilitate a question-and-answer session at the end of the company's remarks.
As a reminder, this conference is being recorded for replay purposes, and the replay will be available on the company's website for one year, as discussed in the company's earnings press release issued yesterday. I will now turn the call over to Mr. Mac Schmitz, Senior Vice President, Investor Relations for Matador. Mr. Schmitz, you may proceed.
Mac Schmitz
SVP of Investor Relations, Matador Resources Company
Thank you, Daniel, and good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us for Matador's Q1 2024 earnings conference call. Some of the presenters today will reference certain non-GAAP financial measures regularly used by Matador Resources in measuring the company's financial performance. Reconciliations of such non-GAAP financial measures with comparable financial measures calculated in accordance with GAAP are contained at the end of the company's earnings press release.
As a reminder, certain statements included in this morning's presentation may be forward-looking and reflect the company's current expectations or forecasts of future events based on information that is now available. Actual results and future events could differ materially from those anticipated in such statements.
Additional information concerning factors that could cause actual results to differ materially is contained in the company's earnings release and its most recent annual report on Form 10-K and any subsequent quarterly reports on Form 10-Q. In addition to this morning's earnings press release, I would like to remind everyone that you can find a slide presentation in connection with the Q1 2024 earnings release under the investor relations tab on our corporate website. With that, I would now like to turn the call over to Mr. Joe Foran, our Founder, Chairman, and CEO. Joe?
Joe Foran
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Matador Resources Company
Thank you, Mac. We'll try to be brief and to the point, but obviously, the quarter is off to a good start. We're really pleased and believe we're confident that the next quarter will be even better. We now have the connectors in place and functioning, so you have 595 miles of pipeline. Their work is enhanced by being in one system.
Second, by doing so, we've increased our flow assurance and not only increased the flow assurance, at the same time, we improved our balance sheet by recently having three transactions. We amended the credit agreement to extend out to 2029, five years and increased the committed amount from $1.325 billion to $1.5 billion, with room to go up from there on the basis of our borrowing base.
That's important because think about it for a moment, that 19 different credit committees among our 19 banks said that we had the financial strength to do that. Then 19 different reservoir groups reviewed our assets and said they were in support of not only the amounts at $1.5 billion, but we could go higher than that.
This what we call the Triple Crown was supported by both our old and new banks and is in place and is available. Not that we plan to spend it immediately or anything else, but it indicates the financial strength that we can look for future quarters. Then the last thing, yes, I'm pleased to report that we're gonna turn on a record number of wells this quarter.
There'll be 43 gross operated wells and 36.2 net wells. I look forward to answering your questions today, but also look forward to coming back in 90 days and indicating what we've done to improve the asset base of Matador. With that, I turn it back to you, Mac, and whatever questions that are on the line.
Mac Schmitz
SVP of Investor Relations, Matador Resources Company
Great. Thanks. Thanks, Joe. Daniel, we're ready for questions. Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. To ask a question, please press star one one on your telephone and wait for your name to be announced. To withdraw your question, please press star one one again. Ladies and gentlemen, due to time constraints, we ask that you please limit yourself to one question and one follow-up. Again, we ask that you please limit yourself to one question and a follow-up until all have had a chance to ask a question. After which, we would welcome additional questions from you. One moment for our first question. Our first question comes from Scott Hanold with RBC Capital Markets. Your line is open.
Scott Hanold
Managing Director of Energy Research, RBC Capital Markets
Hey, thanks. Good morning, y'all. You know, look, brick by brick M&A has been a staple of your strategy, I think, since the inception. I've got sort of a couple part kinda question, but like, how do you see the current, you know, market opportunities in terms of price and quality out there right now? As you go forward, you know, can you talk about the mix, like how you see the economics of, you know, both in organic and inorganic growth? Then finally, if you could give us some color on what you think your financial capacity is to do, you know, more M&A at this point.
Joe Foran
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Matador Resources Company
Well, let me take that in order. You know, the first question is, we're happy to go either way on either growing organically, as we've mainly done, and this Matador has grown primarily organically, but also we're prepared to go by acquisition, depending on whatever the industry and the economy is giving us. You know, there are times when it's better to do one or the other, much like a football team has a passing game and a running game. If you look back, we have now, I think, something like 68 wells that have been drilled on the state line acreage.
Mac Schmitz
SVP of Investor Relations, Matador Resources Company
Yeah. 62 currently producing and then six more this quarter.
Joe Foran
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Matador Resources Company
All right. 68 wells. When we bought that, our stock took a big hit 'cause people couldn't believe we paid that much for it. With 68 wells, you can see that it actually worked out. That's the kind of disadvantage of an acquisition. You pay the upfront money. People can think you've overpaid, and so it takes a matter of months or years to prove it out, just as we did in Stateline.
On the other hand, you have these drilling opportunities, and so you want a balance of those. Again, that takes time, and you do that one at a time. It's an incremental deal over time. There are advantages to both, and the best way to approach them, I believe, is have a wide variety of ways to grow.
You could add midstream into that. Building out midstream is a growth opportunity, organic growth opportunity, but it enhances your product, the value of your production because today, what you need in the Delaware is flow assurance, and there's a capacity limitation.
Unless you have some flow assurance and work with the other pipelines, you're gonna have some difficulties getting your product to market. I just point out that you need to be prepared to grow in any, in all these different ways because you never know what the economy's gonna do or circumstances.
As another example, in the Ice Storm Uri, because we had our own midstream system, those guys I really had respect because they were out there sleeping in their trucks and keeping the gas flowing that might not have occurred elsewhere. Because it was their gas as well as ours, they were out there sleeping in their trucks.
On that point, I just say I think it's helped that we have an employee share purchase plan, which all we have over 90% participation. They're professionals, they would've probably done that anyway, but it didn't discourage them any to keep the gas flowing 'cause they're all shareholders too. Now, your second question was about our financial strength to do this. Is that right, Scott?
Scott Hanold
Managing Director of Energy Research, RBC Capital Markets
Yeah. Just an idea of your capacity to, you know, do more at this point.
Joe Foran
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Matador Resources Company
Well, a good question, thank you for asking. Recently, we did what we called our Triple Crown, we refinanced our reserve-based lending agreement with those 19 banks that I mentioned. We increased it from $1.325 billion to $1.5 billion. As we did that, we've paid down our RBL to where we only have approximately $25 million borrowed on the RBL.
We were able to do that because the RBL was signed on Friday, and on Monday, we did the stock offering for 5 million shares, and that's approximately $350 million. That enabled us to pay down all the RBL. We have, now today, basically $1.5 billion on the RBL available to do acquisitions.
We went out and, on Tuesday, did a bond offering that was heavily oversubscribed, and as was the stock offering, and we picked up $900 million, and those monies aren't due till 2032. We're sitting there with time on our hands. We can afford to be patient, but we're actively looking to grow either way, or a third way with midstream. First Matador grew primarily by acquisition.
The second Matador has been primarily organic. But even acquisitions, we're looking for acreage to go along with whatever production comes. We're not particularly interested in some that's all production. We want a balance between the drill bit and actual production, so that you, in effect, have something that's half organic, half production. Some balance on that. You know, we try to, you know, be creative and solve the problems and work with others. We're active in all those directions.
Scott Hanold
Managing Director of Energy Research, RBC Capital Markets
Great. That I appreciate the color. As my follow-up, Joe, you mentioned flow assurance is important. You know, right now, Waha gas is obviously under pressure and, you know, in the negative kind of arena, and it probably will persist in the back half of this year. Can you talk about your position? Is there any concern of not getting your gas sold or, you know, getting some weak pricing on the residue gas? Can you kinda give us your view of those dynamics for Matador?
Joe Foran
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Matador Resources Company
Well, that's another good question, Scott. I'll let Gregg Krug answer that, who's the head of our marketing and midstream. This is something we've talked a lot about, put a lot of thought into, and I think Gregg's done a terrific job of creating diversity on our sales of our gas product. Gregg?
Gregg Krug
EVP of Marketing and Midstream Strategy, Matador Resources Company
Yeah. Thanks, Joe. Yeah, Scott, we've tried to take a very wide look at this as far as to try to get our diverse market portfolio out there as far as where we're not exposed to one particular index or the other. We've got a lot of different options here, anywhere from hedging to financial positions or gas transport, firm transport, I should say, on takeaway pipelines to other regions, like Houston Ship Channel, for instance. We're looking at all those different options, and I think we've got a pretty good scatter of our exposure to all the different indices.
Joe Foran
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Matador Resources Company
Greg, just to add to that a little bit is that, even at Waha, you have a range that you could either go with or you have other choices. The same thing is that with the NGLs, it gives us a hedge on pricing.
Gregg Krug
EVP of Marketing and Midstream Strategy, Matador Resources Company
Yes. That's correct, Joe. As far as the NGLs, need to keep in mind, you know, we are a two-stream reporter. So, when we talk about our natural gas pricing, we also have an NGL component, and we get a nice uplift on that, you know. It all kind of really all depends on the particular wells, but some of these wells are really rich, and there's a lot of NGL that comes along with the production. So we get a nice uplift on that as well.
Scott Hanold
Managing Director of Energy Research, RBC Capital Markets
Yeah. In particular, just to hone in on one point, if you could, do you have any concerns? I mean, you know, you're growing production in the Permian. It's tight with capacity right now. I don't think a lot of other players are growing production too much, but do you see a risk that, you know, you may not be able to sell your gas, or there'd be difficulty selling your gas that could constrain things, in your outlook at this point?
Gregg Krug
EVP of Marketing and Midstream Strategy, Matador Resources Company
No, we don't. One reason is that, I mean, we do hold firm transport on these pipes. We're protected as far as on the hedging part of it on the basis there at Waha, for instance, where if you see negative pricing there, I mean, we've locked in that basis number for a portion of our gas, where we're not exposed to that with that portion of gas that we've hedged.
I think we've got plenty of transport to get out of the basin. We're not concerned with that. Now, you're right, as far as with growing production that we have, that's one reason we're looking at additional capacity out of the basin, and we're looking at all the different pipes. I think we're well on our way to get in a position where we're gonna be fine on that.
Scott Hanold
Managing Director of Energy Research, RBC Capital Markets
Appreciate it. Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. One moment for our next question. Our next question comes from Tim Rezvan with KeyBanc Capital Markets. Your line is open.
Tim Rezvan
Managing Director and Equity Research Analyst, KeyBanc Capital Markets
Good morning, everybody. Thank you for taking my questions. Just wanted to touch on what Scott was talking about on M&A and more on the bolt-on side. If we look at kind of the cash you raised, you know, for the tender and then the equity issuance, it was much greater than what you spent, you know, in the last couple of quarters on bolt-ons.
Can you provide any kind of line of sight on what you think the bolt-on budget maybe looks like this year? I know it's hard to gauge, but there's a lot of questions about that. Any kind of financial ring-fence you can put around what you see for the rest of the year would be very helpful. Thank you.
Joe Foran
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Matador Resources Company
Tim, I appreciate your question, but it's really difficult to put any number around it all. It's kinda like going fishing, is when you go fishing, you don't know whether you're gonna catch two fish or 10 fish, you know? You're gonna get out there and see what works and what's available and what can be done at a reasonable price.
What I would emphasize that we don't depend on acquisitions to meet our growth targets. Those are opportunistic, and in many cases, we're merely adding to the working interest that we already have. That's kind of the way it works on trades too, is that we trade out of some we don't have a big interest in for something that is more direct on us.
It's really a moving target that we first pin our growth on our drilling activity, where we control the leases and we operate the wells, and then we opportunistically look at the acquisition opportunities, whether it's by trade or by adding working interest from our partners or acquiring a company as we did Advance last year. We've put ourselves this year with that Triple Crown of RBL stock offering and bond offering to where we can do both, meet our drilling growth by drilling and growth by acquisition. We'll do a company when the opportunity is right, but we wanna maintain our ability to go either way.
If you hit a dry spell on acquisitions, you've got plenty of leases to drill, and in that case, we're confident that we could acquire an additional rig or even two to grow organically by drilling that. Our main drilling contractor since the inception of Matador 40 years ago has been Patterson or its predecessors, and we're confident they would work with us to get us the necessary rigs if we needed to do organic growth because the acquisitions have been slim.
The same thing is we're financially in a position that we don't have to cut back on the eight rigs that we currently have running that are high spec-ed to do an acquisition. Because, as I indicated, we've got over $1.5 billion available plus our cash flow, and nothing borrowed on a current RBL, and feel like if we bought some that would only go up with the acquisition. We tried to arrange it, to give us, as we try to say, as many options as we can, Tim.
Tim Rezvan
Managing Director and Equity Research Analyst, KeyBanc Capital Markets
Okay. I was trying for some numbers. I didn't think I'd get it, but I appreciate the context. If I could-
Joe Foran
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Matador Resources Company
Well, Tim, as I would say to you, Tim, as well, everybody else on the call is, look, we'll answer the questions as best we can, but wanna remind you how we run an open shop here, that if you'll come to see us, we'll spend more time with you and let you meet some people. We always want you to know that you and the other analysts are welcome to come here and have a private session with us.
Tim Rezvan
Managing Director and Equity Research Analyst, KeyBanc Capital Markets
Okay. I appreciate that. If I could just change gears on a follow-up on the midstream side. It sounds like things are on track for Marlan for middle of 2025. You know, as a bigger entity, how do you think about kind of long-term large scale projects that you may need to do? If you think you're kind of beyond sort of the heavy lifting on these large projects, how do you weigh the value of owning the segment versus highlighting the value in some potential transaction? Because you could argue there's not a lot of value in the stock today for, you know, San Mateo. I'll leave it there. Thank you.
Joe Foran
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Matador Resources Company
Well, Tim, first, I would say that's a buying opportunity for any shareholder out there that feels we're not getting full value. Because in time, we all know the market begins, you know, in the near term may be a popularity contest, but in the long term it's a weighing deal.
You know, that's why I think you have 90% or more participation by the employees here, 'cause they can see the value of the midstream and the, you know, and the returns that we're getting from our drilling operations. You know, I'm patient on that. I've never sold a share of Matador stock 'cause I could see that the value was increasing. Some of it had not yet been recognized, but in time, I'm confident that it will.
The midstream was done not just as an attraction or that it was done because it had usefulness, utility to our drilling completion and production operations and assured us that we wouldn't be waiting on pipelines, but be getting our gas to market. When that well is ready to come on, there'd be pipe waiting there to take it to market.
Now, it's had additional benefit because of changes in the environmental regulations so that we're not flaring. Over the past four years, we've cut our emissions by 55%, which is partly enabled by having our own pipelines to carry away the water and where we're not having to flare, and we're not trucking the oil and gas and creating that environmental problem. Virtually all of our oil is on top.
It's something I think that adds value, but it also is very useful to our day-to-day operations. I think in time, people will see that. As a public company, we play a straight game. If somebody comes in with a serious offer or a serious proposal in some way, to work with us on our pipeline or, you know, as I said, even to acquire it, we'll give it serious consideration. Right now, we can find plenty of use for it in getting our oil, gas, and water taken away, as needed and is helpful.
Tim Rezvan
Managing Director and Equity Research Analyst, KeyBanc Capital Markets
Thank you.
Joe Foran
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Matador Resources Company
Thank you, Tim.
Operator
One moment for our next question. Our next question comes from Neal Dingmann with Truist Securities. Your line is open.
Neal Dingmann
Managing Director of Energy Research, Truist Securities
Morning, guys. Thanks for the time. Joe and team, nice quarter. Joe, my first question, just on oil services. Maybe ask this a little bit different. Joe, I know you've got great contacts and relationships there. I'm just wondering. I've heard more about what is your thoughts these days, you and the team, about sort of bundling versus de-bundling when it comes to services?
Because I guess where I'm going with that, I've heard as of late there's been sort of pass-through and different costs that have gotten cheaper. So I'm just wondering, when you think about oilfield services. How do you all do you have a preference when it comes to bundling or de-bundling of, you know, the sand, the chems and other things around that?
Joe Foran
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Matador Resources Company
Neal? Yeah. First, I'm just gonna thank our service providers. They've done a terrific job of being there when needed and their efficiency and everything else. Great relationships, and really appreciate the extra effort that we've gotten through them. It's been a team effort, so it's not just us that has gotten things there on time and had the success in the field. They've participated, and they've been great to work with. On specific answer to your question, I'm gonna turn to Chris, and he can tell you how his thoughts on bundling.
Chris Calvert
EVP and COO, Matador Resources Company
Yes. Hi, Neal. IIt's Chris. Chris Calvert, EVP, COO. You know, it's a great topic, you know, and I think one thing that we do like to highlight into is the partnership that we have with Patterson-UTI. Really, if you wanna call it bundling, you know, from a drilling and pressure pumping perspective, that is, I guess, what you would call bundling.
We use two of the largest cost centers that are provided by one parent umbrella company that is Patterson-UTI. You know, they have Universal Pressure Pumping that merged with NexTier. That is really kind of the bundling of two of our largest cost centers. We feel that that is a huge benefit when this transaction took place for the merger between UPP and NexTier.
The services that we were used to with Patterson as far as quality of crews, that carried over. You know, we look at things to where that is really kind of a bundled package within our drilling contractor and our pressure pumping provider. You've mentioned sand and pressure pumping. Similar to our drilling contract, similar to gas takeaway, we always value optionality here as something that we're always going to prioritize.
When you think of sand bundling, whether it is provided by the pressure pumping company or self-sourced through a third party, we continue to look at optionality and the best way to optimize any sort of difference or delta in between contracted volumes from a sand contractor, excuse me, from the pressure pumping provider, or a spot rate that could be a little bit better at any given time.
The value of the optionality between those two services is something that we always look at, but we do bundle that as well at times. It is something that we are always looking at. Those, I think, cover really two of the largest cost centers that we talk to. That's really kinda how we see these things. There are advantages to bundling, and then also it makes sense sometimes to have optionality to where you're not tied to a specific provider.
Neal Dingmann
Managing Director of Energy Research, Truist Securities
That makes a lot of sense. Thanks for the details. Then just a quick follow-up on midstream. With the connections in place now and flow assurance, it seems like everything's really going your way on that. Do you all anticipate more sort of third-party going through that, or should we expect that anytime soon?
Joe Foran
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Matador Resources Company
Yes, Neal. We're developing third-party relations on a constant basis. Our guys are out there meeting and want you know everybody know we run a straight game. One interesting thing that occurred, and Gregg Krug, who's head of our marketing and midstream, can elaborate on it, but one of those third parties said, "I'm very comfortable having you take away the gas and pipeline 'cause I know that if you're flowing, I'm gonna be flowing, and I won't be shut in.
So you know that if you're moving your gas, you gotta be moving my gas, too." We appreciate that perspective, and that's true. We're proud of our third-party people selling the gas, and we try to give them the exact same service that our people get. Neal, so far, they've been most helpful in getting other people to call us to see if we can make a deal on being a reference for us, that they've been real pleased with our service and work. Gregg,
Gregg Krug
EVP of Marketing and Midstream Strategy, Matador Resources Company
This is Gregg again. I echo what Joe just said as far as we definitely do not play favorites when it comes to Matador gas over our third party that we have out there. I think that's critical that we do that. We wanna stay credible. That's not the way to treat your third party whenever you've got them on your system. We definitely try to treat them the same as the Matador gas. It is a comfort, I think, to some of them as far as that. That's one thing we have heard as far as that. We're gonna go the extra effort to make sure gas flows during bad storms.
Joe just talked about Winter Storm Uri. That's a good example of that. We, our folks were out there day and night, and I mean nighttime too, actually working during subfreezing weather. You know, I can't say that necessarily about some of the other folks out there, as far as the other midstream companies and so forth, 'cause we did have some shut-ins on some of the wells we had connected to other places. That is, I feel like there's some assurance there for third parties.
Joe Foran
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Matador Resources Company
Yeah. On that same note, we're comforted by the amount of repeat business. Virtually all of our current third-party customers are repeat customers. They've been with us before. Let me turn it to Glenn, who's the head of our production-
Glenn Stetson
EVP of Production, Matador Resources Company
Yes.
Joe Foran
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Matador Resources Company
That is making that happen.
Glenn Stetson
EVP of Production, Matador Resources Company
Yeah. Neal, I just wanted to kind of pile on here and give a shout-out to the guys in the field. You know, Sam Witten and Paul Ramirez were a big part of getting those connectors driven to completion, you know, on time or ahead of time and on budget.
You know, those connectors, you know, in the quarter, we installed over 50 miles of pipe, and we talked about some of the oilfield service side. You know, our guys in the field work very closely with the companies that construct those pipelines. We were able to do quite a bit of work in Q1, and it sets us up very nicely for Q2.
We have a number of wells that are going to produce to utilize those connectors, including those 21 Dagger Lake South wells. It was a very busy quarter and again, kind of sets us up really nicely here for Q2.
Neal Dingmann
Managing Director of Energy Research, Truist Securities
Great details. Thanks, Joe. Thanks, team.
Joe Foran
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Matador Resources Company
Thanks, Neal.
Tom Elsener
EVP of Reservoir Engineering and Senior Asset Manager, Matador Resources Company
Thanks, Neal.
Operator
Thank you. One moment for our next question. Our next question comes from Zach Parham with JPMorgan. Your line is open.
Zach Parham
Executive Director of US E&P, Oil and Gas Equity Research, JPMorgan
Hey, guys. Thanks for taking my question. You highlighted that higher oil volumes were driven by better than expected production at Stateline. I noticed you hadn't turned in line any wells there since Q2 of last year. Just trying to get a little bit more color on what's driving the outperformance there. Is it shallower declines than you would have thought? Maybe just any color you can provide there on the better performance.
Tom Elsener
EVP of Reservoir Engineering and Senior Asset Manager, Matador Resources Company
Hey, Zach, it's Tom Elsener. Yeah, thank you for your question. It's a great question. You know, I think a lot of the performance has been due to, you know, really on the Midstream team. Again, I know we've talked about that quite a bit, but they have a unique system that they designed down at Stateline that Glenn can talk about more.
Basically, they are able to custom put these wells into either a high-pressure, medium-pressure, or low-pressure gathering system that allows them to very rapidly appropriately fit the wells to the pipeline pressure. The lower pressure they can go into, the better the wells can produce. That also aids in our ability to recover from offset activity, if wells go down and need repairs.
There's a lot of, you know, clever things that Glenn and his team and work with the same team have been able to accomplish down there. They're certainly great wells, and we're very proud of them as well. You know, I think a lot of the, you know, the comments you made, you know, here recently have been to the credit of the Midstream team. I will say we have drilled 6 additional wells, and those will be online here later in Q2 as well.
Zach Parham
Executive Director of US E&P, Oil and Gas Equity Research, JPMorgan
Got it. Thanks for that color. And then just one on the guidance. You raised the full-year guidance to the high end of the range, but didn't provide an update on the Q4 exit rate guidance, which was previously, I think, 98,000 bpd at the high end. Just trying to get a sense of the production trajectory going forward. You know, based on my math, to get to the high end of the range in 2024, it seemed like you're just over 100,000 bpd in Q4. Maybe if you could just give us an update on where you expect to exit the year and maybe any initial thoughts on what that could mean for 2025 volumes.
Brian J. Willey
EVP and CFO, Matador Resources Company
Yeah, Zach, this is Brian. Happy to answer that. Thanks for the question. You know, you're right, we pointed to the high end of guidance. We're really proud of the quarter that we had and to be able to point to the high end of guidance for the year. I mean, fantastic work by the teams and be able to execute that. We haven't given a lot of specifics on the H2 of the year, whether, you know, the balance between Q3 and Q4. I think there's a lot of golf to be played there. You know, I think expect Q3 to continue to improve over Q2. Then as it relates to Q4, obviously, it's, you know, a few months out and we're early in the year.
We haven't updated the guidance as it relates to that quarter yet. You know, we're really excited about the remainder of the year and how it sets us up for a great 2024 and then into 2025. Just really, really great news all around.
Zach Parham
Executive Director of US E&P, Oil and Gas Equity Research, JPMorgan
Okay. Thank you, guys.
Joe Foran
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Matador Resources Company
Thanks, Zach.
Operator
Thank you. Our final question comes from the line of Leo Mariani with Roth. Your line is open.
Leo Mariani
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, ROTH MKM
Hey, guys. Wanted to just ask a little bit on CapEx trajectory here. Wanting to get a sense of how you see that kind of playing out. I know you've got the Q2 guidance here. Would you guys expect CapEx to come down a bit in H2 of the year versus you know H1? Just trying to kind of get a sense of the capital cadence as it kind of relates to the operations.
Joe Foran
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Matador Resources Company
Leo, that's a great question, and we talk about it every week, if not every day, of how things are looking. It's a little hard to predict because somewhat tied to what the commodity price is to it. If the commodity price goes up, our current estimates would be a little low. If it goes down, then our CapEx estimates are probably gonna be a little high.
Now that's simplistic, but we try to put the best number we can and adjust it throughout the year. You know, stay within cash flow and the other financial parameters that we make our decisions by. Let me turn it to Brian Willey, because he works on this every day, if not every hour.
Brian J. Willey
EVP and CFO, Matador Resources Company
Thanks, Joe. It certainly feels like every hour. It's not every minute. No, we think about this a lot, as Joe said, and talk about that. You're right, Leo. We did point to the high end of guidance for production, but we're proud that we were able to do that and not change our guidance as it relates to capital expenditures. You saw in our release, we had $10 million that was in savings that we incurred during Q1.
Great job by Chris and his team, the production group as well, and just really great execution. The remainder was just shifted into Q2, and we expect throughout the remainder of the year that kind of midpoint of guidance on the CapEx. You'll see that just play out over the Q3 and then in the Q4. You know, really excited to be able to raise production guidance while we didn't change CapEx guidance. I think that's a great story for us.
Joe Foran
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Matador Resources Company
Leo, that's the way I look at it. It's a two variable deal. It's not just what are you going to spend, but what are you gonna get for that money that you've spent. That's why Brian's point, I think, is a real good one, that we increased production, but we didn't increase CapEx, which meant we were able to achieve some cost savings as well as to find ways to improve our efficiency.
We'll continue that throughout the year. While it may vary a little bit, we'll be matching it up or comparing it to what we're getting accomplished in the way of increased production or increased services or, you know, fixed plant like the Marlan. All that goes in, and I look upon it as a two variable deal as opposed to a one variable.
Leo Mariani
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, ROTH MKM
Okay. No, I appreciate that. Just wanted to follow up on the midstream here. Joe, you certainly mentioned that you thought there was some, you know, hidden value in the stock, and you could be, you know, somewhat patient and maybe wait for a deal at some point. You know, I know that, you know, Matador's or companies maybe expressed a little bit of frustration over the last year or so that all the midstream value creation hasn't, you know, shown up in the stock.
I mean, I guess to the extent that, you know, we kinda continue on and later this year or into next year and you still feel like there's not a lot of value in the stock, is Matador maybe poised at some point to maybe take some action to try to bring some of that value out on the midstream side?
Joe Foran
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Matador Resources Company
Well, you know, we're always looking for opportunities. As I said, we're a public company, and people that have proposals, we will look at them. If they're serious proposals, we'll look at them very seriously. While I, you know, I think everybody runs a company would like, feels their stock is a little, underpriced, I don't know very many CEOs get out there and say, "Hey, guys, our stock's overpriced.
You might wanna trim a little bit." Yes, I think there are opportunities. You look at us, how we've outperformed overall, how we've outperformed the S&P 500 or the Russell 2000 or even our peers, we've been one of the highest performing. Like anybody, you're always looking to do a little better.
If you can think that the first Matador started with $270,000. After 20 years, we sold for $388 million. It was a nice run. This Matador started at $6 million, and we're, you know, up there over $8 billion, approaching $9 billion. An original shareholder in the first Matador got in at $0.85, $0.90, something like that, and sold for $18.25.
This Matador, their basis of the original shareholder is $3.56. Now we're in the $60s. You know, that's been a pretty good return. During COVID, we went down to single digits, and anybody that bought then has had a 10-to-one type gain. Now we're paying a dividend.
It really doesn't matter so much what it was, but what is it now to someone and what could they might expect. If it behaves like we've done the last 40 years, it's still gonna be a very good return for them, and continue to be a good run.
I mean, but going from $3.56 back in 2003 to 65 is a, you know, basically a 20-to-one. Even if you're not getting 100% of the quote, whatever you call true value, you still have the benefit of over a 20-to-one type gain, and we're paying a dividend now that has grown steadily since we've done it. We think that's a good offering.
If you look at the quality of the properties, you know, we feel like we're in the best basin, earning good return, have expanded to, you know, hedge our value some by having a midstream. You not only have a commodity-based business, but you have a fee-based business. That also reduces the risk. You look at the heavy ownership by employees, and again, I repeat, I've never sold a share of stock, so, and neither have most of our other officers 'cause we can see the opportunity is growing, and sooner or later, if we really have the value that we think we have, those in the market will see it and come on.
One of the major business magazines in the country, you would all know if I mentioned the title, had an article that said we were one of the eight stocks that people ought to buy. The other companies that they mentioned in there were far better known than us, General Motors being one of them. If you look at that article, I was flattered to be in that group. I think the outlook is good. We've been very consistent. You look at how many quarters that we've met or exceeded guidance, I think, and the financial strength that we have, the oversubscriptions that we had both on the stock and the bond, is another good sign.
When you figure 19 different banks have their credit committees look at it and say, "This looks fine." They have 19 different reservoir groups. I think we've been thoroughly vetted as some that has some value. I think both our drilling side and our midstream side are very optimistic that they'll be continuing to add value in the years ahead.
Our team has depth, and they're really working well together. As we said, we've been giving, you know, throwing praises on our field guys because we think they're some of the best in the business, and I think the staff is. It's really a total team effort, and they're not sharp elbows, but just a bunch of guys that are trying to add value.
We've grown, as I said, from nothing, basically nothing to being the number eight largest company in New Mexico. I think it's a pretty good record. Past performance is no guarantee of future performance, but that's why I like to bet, and I like our chances.
Leo Mariani
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, ROTH MKM
Okay. Appreciate all the questions.
Joe Foran
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Matador Resources Company
Ask me how I really feel.
Leo Mariani
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, ROTH MKM
Thank you.
Joe Foran
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Matador Resources Company
Thank you. Come see us.
Leo Mariani
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, ROTH MKM
Will do.
Operator
Thank you. Ladies and gentlemen, this ends the Q&A portion of this morning's conference call. I'd like to turn the call over to management for any closing remarks.
Joe Foran
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Matador Resources Company
Well, after that last speech, I think I'll just say ditto and tell you we really appreciate y'all listening in. The invitation to come see us and visit more at length in more detail about any questions you have is open, is sincere, and we mean it. I think as you meet our people, you'll feel more and more comfortable with either investing or adding to your investment.
I also want to note that we have an annual meeting coming up 13 June 2024, I believe, and we would invite you to attend the annual meeting. It's a little different than some because we didn't come up through private equity, but we came up through friends and family. You have a lot of individual investors that are there that have been shareholders for 40 years.
You know, as long as 40 years and many that are in the 20 to 30 years, you can ask about their experience. You have a chance to visit with our young people and take an estimate of what you think of them. They'll be there with displays about the new drilling bits that are coming onto the market and other bits of innovation as the U-turn wells and explain how that comes about, as well as other things we get questioned.
Really think that's an opportunity that you may not get with larger companies that are more formal. You know, we really invite you. We'd like to get to know y'all better and continue to have more dialogue. Brian invites you and Van and our president. Let me turn it to our president. Van, what would you add to all this?
Van Singleton II
President of Land, A&D and Planning, Matador Resources Company
I think, Joe, one thing I would add is just obviously everyone on the phone can't see the room, but the room is full with our team and the staff, and really wanna thank everybody in the room, everyone in the whole company, because these are good results, and those results wouldn't happen if everyone weren't doing their part and pitching in and working together.
So also thank you to you know some of these companies that we've done deals with. We feel like we try to structure our deals as win-win for both sides, and a lot of those companies are repeat business. We get back together when there's another deal to do. So it really is all about relationships. We do cherish our relationships, and Joe's invitation is sincere.
We do hope to see everybody when you get a chance, or at least talk on the phone more if you come up with other questions. Thank everyone for pitching in and doing their part, and we'll keep running headlong into the next quarter.
Joe Foran
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Matador Resources Company
Yeah. I would like to say there's 50, over 50 people besides the senior officers here in this room, and we do that so everybody knows what's going on and has an idea of where we go from here, and they get to hear your questions, and they like to hear my answers and the answers of the other senior people. It's a little different than some companies do, but it works for us, having come up again with friends and family.
We've tried to maintain that availability, and we think y'all's helped make us better with your questions and the like, because afterwards we go over the questions and make sure that we're addressing them. Y'all have often made really good points that we've taken into consideration in making our final decisions. Thank you. I think it's a process that works. Maybe a little slow at times, but we'll get there and we like our chances going ahead. Come see us and keep in touch.
Operator
Ladies and gentlemen, thank you for your participation today. This concludes today's program.

content.text:
Operator
Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Welcome to the Q3 2023 Matador Resources Company Earnings Conference Call. My name is Latif, and I'll be serving as the operator for today. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. We will facilitate a question-and-answer session at the end of the company's remarks. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded for replay purposes, and the replay will be available on the company's website for one year, as discussed in the company's earnings press release issued yesterday. I will now turn the call over to Mr. Mac Schmitz, Vice President, Investor Relations for Matador. Mr. Schmitz, you may proceed. Mr. Schmitz, your line is open, sir.
Mac Schmitz
VP of Investor Relations, Matador Resources
Thank you, Latif, and good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us for Matador's Q3 2023 Earnings Conference Call. Some of the presenters today will reference certain non-GAAP financial measures regularly used by Matador Resources in measuring the company's financial performance. Reconciliations of such non-GAAP financial measures with the comparable financial measures calculated in accordance with GAAP are contained at the end of the company's earnings press release. As a reminder, certain statements included in this morning's presentation may be forward-looking and reflect the company's current expectations or forecasts of future events based on the information that is now available. Actual results and future events could differ materially from those anticipated in such statements.
Additional information concerning factors that could cause actual results to differ materially is contained in the company's earnings release and its most recent annual report on Form 10-K and any subsequent quarterly reports on Form 10-Q. In addition to our earnings press release, I would like to remind everyone on the call that you can find a slide presentation in connection with the Q3 2023 earnings release under the Investor Relations tab on our corporate website. With that, I would now like to turn the call over to Mr. Joe Foran, our Founder, Chairman, and CEO. Joe?
Joe Foran
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Matador Resources
Thank you, Mac, and thank you all for listening in. It's a pleasure to be here today and a pleasure to give you this report. In very simplest terms, we said at the beginning of the year that we began the year at 100,000 BOE equivalent, and we're gonna finish the year at 140,000 BOE. I was wrong. It's gonna be 145,000 BOE. We're pleased to report, in addition to production being up, our debt is down, costs are down, and we think our opportunities are also up, that the plans that we put into place are proceeding as expected or better than expected. We're excited to report this to you and look for your questions.
We feel we've ended the year 2023 with more inventory, more options, and the outlook for 2024 is even better. As strong as this year is, you know, I repeat that 2024 is better. I would point to you. I had two slides in the materials, the first one shows our performance over the last five years against our peers, as selected. We feel like we've outperformed them. The second one is more interesting, our performance since the IPO. The team has made great strides. I give them the credit. People are really working well together. They've come up with good ideas, and Matador has continued to grow.
When we went public, we were about $300 million, and today the market cap is somewhere around $7.5 billion. But should get better as the year goes along. We've given projections, but they are confident they will all be realized. I think on slide B, something that struck me as we prepared this was that three times we have announced what were very meaningful deals to us. The first one was the HEYCO deal, and immediately announcing it, we thought, anticipating it'd go up, but things went down, which was a big surprise to us. Then when we bought the BLM leases, again, we thought the market would easily recognize the potential of these wells.
We have now drilled close to 90 wells on these leases, but instead of going up, things plunged. In this deal, besides 98 wells happening and the production from them, it enabled us to go from 98% of our wells being one-mile laterals to 98% of our wells being 2 miles or more, and you see the dramatic effect of that. Right after that, as things started to stabilize, we ran into COVID, and things plunged again. As we turned on the state line wells, and these wells were paying out in less than a year, at some even paid out at $20 a barrel, you can see where that's taken us to much higher levels. Again, the third time was the charm.
We had announced the advanced deal, and instead of going up, it went down again. Since then, things have been going good for us. As you can see, as we've increased the production, as I mentioned, first of the year, 100,000 BOE, end of the year, pretty simple math, 145,000 BOE, we're headed in the right direction. Now, just again, a brief history of our Delaware position. We started it when we went public in 2012. At that time, we had six wells. This is slide C. Five years later, in 2017, we had 212 wells. Now in 2023, we've got 751 wells. Our market cap has increased and all the other important categories have too, including the dividend. It's with pleasure, we like dividends here.
I would like to emphasize that. We're all large shareholders, and over 95% of our employees are participating in the employee purchase plan of our stock. I appreciate the vote of confidence from the staff. We're gonna try to deliver. Again, pleased that we've had four raises of the dividend, and now we're at $0.80. The other progress is you get into it. We've got production up, our costs are down. We think our inventory selection is better than ever, and debt is down $200 million. We're at $500 million. We have almost $1 billion in availability under our RBL with our bank group.

Rob Macalik
EVP and Chief Accounting Officer, Matador Resources
Leo, this is Rob Macalik. I'm the EVP and Chief Accounting Officer. Two things kind of moved in our favor since the last quarter. One of those, we estimated higher 2023 revenue, both because of production and price, and we had lower operating and capital cost estimates for the year. So that led to a little bit higher estimated taxable income and thus our estimate of about a 1% cash tax payment that we'll make for the year. We're obviously doing everything we can to plan for that and to work on our deductions that we can to minimize our income tax payments. For 2024, there are a few things that we're still analyzing and studying.
In addition to the plans for the year, we're also waiting for IRS guidance on the corporate alternative minimum tax, which would be a 15% book tax. We think there are several things in the guidance that we're waiting for that we're going to be able to do better than that.
Okay. That's helpful, guys. I was also hoping to see if you guys could follow up a little bit on M&A. There's obviously been some significant deals done in the Permian here in 2023. You guys obviously did one of those, you know, with the Advance deal. How are you kind of thinking about it going forward? Do you think the focus is kind of more ground game, you know, kind of brick by brick approach here? Or do you think that there may be some larger deals that Matador could eventually be involved in?
Joe Foran
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Matador Resources
Well, this is Joe, and I'd emphasize that it's like being in a football game. Are you gonna run more or are you gonna pass more? It all depends on the opportunities and how things go. We try to make sure we have enough of a ground game every year that we're gonna hit our growth and production increase, free cash flow increase, pay down debt, and do all those essentials. On the acquisition side, you know, we tend to just be opportunistic. We don't do a lot, but you can see in our history that when we've done deals, they've been accretive to what we're trying to do and has enhanced the ground game.
We're open to acquire. We're more of an acquirer than we are a seller, but we're very open to buying something, but we want it to make sense. We're not trying to get bigger as much as we're trying to get better, and to acquire interest in our existing wells from people or something like that has a fit to our acreage positions or our midstream. We're always open for deals. Van, can you comment? You're our lead guy on this.
Van Singleton
President of Land, Acquisitions, Divestiture and Planning, Matador Resources
Yeah. Joe, I think, you know, what you're saying is right, and I think you guys have heard this from us, for a decade or so, that we're always on the lookout for good deals. We're gonna make sure that we keep the balance sheet strong. When opportunities present themselves that we feel like are gonna give our acreage position an enhancement, whether it be in existing units or expanding into new units, we're gonna take a hard look at it, and if the deal's right, we'll do it. I think Joe's right. We're buyers, and we're always looking.
Joe Foran
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Matador Resources
Thanks.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Trafford Lamar of Raymond James.
Trafford Lamar
Equity Research Analyst, Raymond James
Hi, guys. Thanks for taking my questions. The first one I have, it circles around the horseshoe wells. How did the cycle times on these wells compare to your more standard two-mile laterals? Any color on that would be great.
Chris Calvert
EVP and Co-COO, Matador Resources
Hi, Trafford. This is Chris Calvert, again, EVP, Co-COO. You know, I think cycle times, when we look at these, I wanna always remind people these were part of a larger nine-well batch, these two horseshoe wells. You know, from a reference point, for example, looking back to a previous, you know, our previous record for drilling a two-mile Wolfcamp A in our Wolf asset area, you know, one of these horseshoes actually beat that record by about 20% from a spud to spud to TD. You know, when you think about just cycle times, it's hard to put a number on it because it's highly dependent on the quantity of wells within the batch. But from just drilling times, completion times, you know, they're very comparable to a straight two-mile lateral.
You know, I think we kinda like to joke. The drill bit doesn't necessarily know it's drilling a U-turn. It just, you know, with the new technologies, whether it's new bit technologies, new motor technologies, we continue to go out and perform, whether it's a U-turn well like we did on this or other 2mi, 2.5mi, and even 2.7mi that we're looking to put online here in the next year. It's just always about continuing to drill fast and reduce those cycle times.
Trafford Lamar
Equity Research Analyst, Raymond James
Perfect. Appreciate that, Chris. Just a quick one here just to clarify. Have you all already signed the contract and secured the additional eight rig for Q1 2024, or is that happening later this quarter?
Chris Calvert
EVP and Co-COO, Matador Resources
This is Chris again. It's likely to happen in the short term in the next week or two, few weeks, whatever it could be. Once again, leaning into and valuing the relationship with Patterson-UTI, it is right now we have an understanding that we will be adding a rig in Q1 next year. You know, obviously highly predicated on the super-spec capabilities of that rig to make sure it's drilling wells in a manner that we've grown used to. That's kind of the storyline there.
Trafford Lamar
Equity Research Analyst, Raymond James
Great. Appreciate it. Thanks, guys.
Van Singleton
President of Land, Acquisitions, Divestiture and Planning, Matador Resources
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Kevin MacCurdy of Pickering Energy Partners.
Kevin MacCurdy
Director, Pickering Energy Partners
Hey, good morning, Joe and team. Just one question for me today. We noticed realized oil prices have gone back to being above WTI, both through actuals in Q3 and the guidance for Q4. I wonder if you could talk about what you're seeing there that has improved over the first couple quarters earlier this year.
Brian Willey
CFO, Matador Resources
Yeah. This is Brian, and I think Greg can feel free to chime in as well. You know, I think just looking at the price of oil, I think part of it's the roll as we've looked at this historically and just how the price is calculated and the realized pricing. That's something that we saw an impact from, you know, looking at Q2 to Q3 and even Q1 to Q2. I think as we look forward going, you know, into the future, I think that's a big piece of it is, and just how the roll plays an effect in the realized pricing.
Also, I'll just say, I think one of the big benefits we have is that a lot of the marketing team's done a very good job in getting much of our oil on pipe. I think that's really significant because we are able to save a cost there and be able to incur those savings there by getting a higher realized price. But Gregg, I don't know if you got anything else you wanted to add.
Joe Foran
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Matador Resources
Well, yeah. I think as far as the amount of oil on pipe, it also helps, you know, versus being trucked. It's a lot more efficient. It helps the operations as well, streamline that. That's a big benefit to be able to have as much oil on pipe as we do.
Leo Mariani
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, ROTH MKM
I'll just add that, yesterday, we put out our sustainability report.
Joe Foran
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Matador Resources
Give credit to the team that built that together. I think it's in good shape. Makes for good nighttime reading. It is good reference material. You know, take a look at that. We've worked hard to put more and more on pipe and to reduce our emissions by 44%.
Shelley Alpern
Director and Former ESG Coordinator, Matador Resources
Sure. This is Shelley Alpern, Director and Former ESG Coordinator. I will say that in 2022, we had 89% of our operated produced oil on pipe. To Joe's point, we're very, very pleased that from 2019 to 2022, we reduced our greenhouse gas intensity by 44%, so almost cutting it in half over that four-year period.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from Oliver Huang of TPH&Co.
Oliver Huang
Associate, TPH&Co
Good morning, all, and thanks for taking my questions. My first question, just, with respect to the Arrowhead area. I know there's a significant portion of your Q4 program in New Mexico coming from there. I assume these wells should be online in pretty short order, but I was just trying to get a better understanding on plans for getting those wells online. Is the thinking there something similar to kind of the staggered nature we saw out of the Margarita wells, in that Advance area last quarter?
Tom Elsener
EVP of Reservoir Engineering and Senior Asset Manager, Matador Resources
Oliver, thanks for the question. This is Tom Elsener again. You know, as we usually do with large batches of wells, we typically would bring them online in some sort of staggered fashion. You know, some of the wells could use artificial lift, you know, at varying times. You know, again, this is something we've historically done, you know, all throughout the basin, whether that's, you know, State Line or Rodney or any other. There are other kind of large batches of wells. We're very excited for these wells. This is an area that, you know, we've been building up to for many years, getting these targets ready, making sure that, you know, San Mateo and the team are up there.
I know, you know, Glenn and the team are excited to get these wells up and running.
Glenn Stetson
EVP of Production, Matador Resources
Yeah. Oliver, this is Glenn. I'd just add that the 17 wells are gonna come in at different times, and they're actually on different development units and delivered to different facilities. A little bit different than the Advance situation where you had 21 wells going to one facility. But Tom, just what Tom said is exactly accurate. We'll bring them on, you know, a few at a time. Then, you know, they're all delivering to San Mateo oil, gas, and water. We'll help bolster volumes there.
Oliver Huang
Associate, TPH&Co
Awesome. That's helpful. Just for a second question. I know in the past you all have called out activity or even certain pads that might require incremental downtime or shut-ins. I'm just kinda thinking about this next batch of 20 or so wells in the Advance area in early 2024. Are we gonna need to see some of the recently online Margarita wells either being curtailed or shut in when those come online on the backdrop of, I guess, tighter infrastructure? Not sure if the next set of wells is far enough in proximity within Ranger to where such impacts might be deemed relatively minimal, but really just trying to understand that dynamic as well as we enter next year.
Glenn Stetson
EVP of Production, Matador Resources
Oliver, this is Glenn again. The short answer is no. The Dagger Lake South development of those additional 21 wells are not in proximity to the Margarita wells. The nature of shutting in wells for offset frack protection won't be a situation on this particular development.
Zach Parham
VP and Executive Director, JPMorgan
Awesome. Thanks for the time.
Glenn Stetson
EVP of Production, Matador Resources
Yep.
Operator
Thank you, ladies and gentlemen. This ends the Q&A portion of this morning's conference call. I'd like to turn the call over to management for any closing remarks.
Joe Foran
Founder, Chairman, and CEO, Matador Resources
Well, thanks to everyone for their time and attention in this. I would like to emphasize the fundamentals. I've said it once already. We started the year at 100,000bbl. We're gonna end the year not just at 140,000bbl but 145,000bbl. That's 40% to 45% growth. Meanwhile, we reduced the debt over $200 million from this while we were keeping those rigs busy and bringing those wells online. In addition, Glenn reduced LOE expenses. Through time, we reduced our drilling cost per foot in a time of rising service cost. We've continued to build out the midstream opportunities, improved ESG. I think it's been a really good year to this point and a really good quarter.
As you know, the stock is off during trading. I admit, but I think it's a buying opportunity, and I've never sold a single share of my stock during the 12 years that we've been public, and so have most of the other officers. If you look at it, we're buyers of stock and not sellers, and we have great participation from our staff. I think anybody who buys at this point is gonna be real pleased with the final year's outcome. I can understand you would like to have us have exact numbers as we think things are gonna be, but that's not the long-term right thing to do, nor is it prudent in a time of such volatility. We can tell you that we're gonna be profitable.
We're gonna keep that leverage ratio less than one, unless some spectacular opportunity shows itself. But every moment is to keep the balance sheet strong, production growing, costs coming down, and continued good execution. We think midstream enhances our opportunity because it assures us of flow assurance. As I often said to people on the road, that if you're gonna be a cotton farmer in Dawson County, you need to own part of the cotton gin. The midstream purchase is that same deal. If you wanna get your cotton processed properly, own part of the cotton gin. We think that midstream has come in to deliver efficiencies and predictability to what we're doing. We haven't missed on anything.
We just had to have detail for you, and that's coming, but we can't do it with full confidence until things settle down a little bit. Take another look at the fundamentals and come see us. We invite all of you. If you want a more thorough discussion and more time with our senior people, come see us. We'll set you up and make sure you leave with all your questions answered that we're allowed to under the SEC rules. We play a straight game, but we're happy to go in further detail on your questions if you can make it here. We'd like to get to know y'all better. I think you can see that we have strength in areas.
Our properties are getting better, our people are getting better, and, you know, the outlook continues to get better. That's what I'd like to end on with a personal invitation to come see us. Who I didn't get to speak to today is Ned, our head of our geoscience group, and the outlook for them on working with the acreage that we have, the number of locations, and the inventory continues to grow, you know, 10, 15, 20 years out, that we see that coming, and their work and staying in zone all contribute to these good results.
We wouldn't have raised dividends if we thought our future was weak, and we wouldn't have gotten the increase in our reserve-based loans that we did from the banks, unless they saw that we had plenty of reserves and inventory and we're headed in the right direction financially. With that, I'd like to thank you again for your time and attention and tell you we look forward to getting with you the next time. We'll have more detail, but we're gonna still maintain our flexibility and options, 'cause at our size, we think one of our strengths is trying to be nimble enough to take advantage of opportunities as they come up, rather than trying to give a five-year outlook. Too much change occurs, and what's served us well is being able to adapt to the changing circumstances.
Come see us. This is a great team and great properties, and we'll go into greater depth. Thanks.
Operator
Ladies and gentlemen, thank you for your participation today. This concludes today's program.
